opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most exciting thing about AlphaEvolve is how general the recipe is. At its core, you have a large language model proposing changes to code, and an automated evaluator that tells you whether those changes actually made things better. That loop — propose, evaluate, keep the best ideas, and evolve them further — doesn't really care what domain you're in. As long as you can express your problem as code and write down a way to score a candidate solution, you can point the system at it.

So in mathematics, for example, we've used it on open problems where you're searching for a construction — some object that beats the best known bound. Historically that's been painstaking work, often requiring a lot of clever, bespoke search code written by hand. With AlphaEvolve, a mathematician can set up the problem, and the system explores a huge space of programs that generate candidate constructions. In a number of cases it matched the state of the art, and in some it actually improved on it.

In computer science, it's found faster algorithms — the matrix multiplication result is one example people have latched onto. And then there's a very practical side: we've applied it inside Google to things like data center scheduling, kernel optimization for training models, even hardware design. Those are areas where a small percentage improvement translates into real resources saved.

Looking across fields, I think the shift is less about AI replacing scientists and more about changing what a scientist spends their time on. Instead of hand-crafting every heuristic, the expert's job becomes defining the problem well — what are we optimizing, what does a good answer look like — and then letting the system do a much broader, more creative search than any one person could. Fields with a clear notion of evaluation, like math, algorithm design, and engineering, are the natural first beneficiaries. The open frontier is extending this to areas where evaluation is noisier or more expensive, like experimental sciences, where you might need simulations or even lab results in the loop. That's where I think a lot of the interesting work over the next few years is going to be.

r003.rationale: It describes exploring a large space of programs that generate candidate constructions and says the system performs a broad search over candidate solutions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the thing that excites me most about AlphaEvolve is that it's quite a general tool. At its core, it's a system that takes a problem you can describe in code and evaluate automatically, and then it uses a language model to propose variations, keeps the ones that score better, and iterates. That loop is simple, but it turns out to apply to a surprisingly wide range of things.

So on the mathematics side, we've used it on problems like matrix multiplication, where it found an algorithm for multiplying four-by-four complex matrices with fewer scalar multiplications than had been known since Strassen's work in 1969. And it's found new constructions in combinatorics and geometry, things like the kissing number problem in eleven dimensions, or packing problems, where it improved on bounds that people had been working on for decades.

But the same system also went after practical engineering problems inside Google. It found a scheduling heuristic for our data centers that recovers a meaningful fraction of compute, it helped simplify a circuit in a TPU design, and it sped up parts of the kernels used to train Gemini itself. So you have this one piece of machinery that moves between pure mathematics and infrastructure without really changing.

What I think this points to for science more broadly is a shift in where the human effort goes. The scientist's job becomes framing the problem well, defining what a good solution looks like so it can be measured, and then interpreting what comes back. The search over the space of candidate solutions, which has historically been slow and heavily reliant on intuition, becomes something the system can do at scale, exploring far more ideas than any individual could.

I'd also stress that the outputs are legible. These aren't black-box predictions, they're programs you can read, verify, and build on. That matters a lot for scientific trust. A mathematician can check the construction. An engineer can read the heuristic and understand why it works.

And honestly, I think we're at an early stage. The fields where this is immediately useful are the ones where you can write a fast, reliable evaluator. The interesting frontier is extending that to domains where evaluation is expensive or noisy, like biology or materials, and figuring out how the human and the system collaborate there.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting shift is that AI can participate in the loop of discovery: proposing an idea, testing it, seeing what happens, and using that feedback to propose something better.

With a system like AlphaEvolve, the key question is: can you evaluate a candidate reliably? In mathematics, that might mean checking whether a construction satisfies certain conditions. In computer science, it might mean running an algorithm and measuring its performance. When that feedback is cheap and precise, you can explore a very large space of possibilities.

In fields where you need a physical experiment, the loop is harder. You have to think about the cost of each experiment, how long it takes, and whether your simulation captures what matters in the real world. So I wouldn’t expect the impact to look identical across disciplines.

But there’s a common opportunity here. Scientists can define the questions and constraints, and these systems can help explore possibilities that would be difficult to search manually. Then there’s another important step: understanding why a discovery works. Finding a better solution and turning it into scientific understanding are related, but they’re distinct accomplishments.

r003.rationale: It describes proposing candidates, testing them, learning from feedback, and exploring a large space of possibilities, framing discovery as a search process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting shift is that AI can participate in the discovery loop. You propose an idea, test it, look at the result, and use that feedback to decide what to try next. With systems like AlphaEvolve, you can start to automate parts of that process, particularly when the ideas can be expressed as code and evaluated reliably.

That applies across quite different fields. In mathematics, you might search for a construction with particular properties. In computer science, you might look for a better algorithm. In engineering, you might optimize a design under constraints. The underlying pattern is similar, even though the objects you’re searching over are different.

The big distinction is how you get feedback. If you can check a candidate quickly on a computer, you can explore a lot of possibilities. If every test requires a physical experiment, that loop becomes much more expensive, and choosing the right experiment matters enormously.

So I see these systems as expanding what scientists can explore. But the scientist still has a crucial role in choosing the question, defining what counts as progress, and understanding whether a result tells us something interesting about the world.
